items.title: Body Schema Policy: Body as the Vision-Action Interface for Efficient Robot Loco-Manipulation
items.abstract: Currently, robots can learn whole-body loco-manipulation through scale: the strongest policies have billions of parameters and still need task-specific fine-tuning. Humans have limited processing capacity, yet learn and act efficiently through a body schema that organizes what they see and how they move. We introduce Body Schema Policy (BSP), an imitation learning policy that builds such a schema into the vision-action interface. Its latent body schema places joint and link tokens on the robot's kinematic tree, where learned screw motions carry features between links. Through body-queried vision, each body part retrieves its own visual evidence, which conditions the denoising of its actions. With this inductive bias, BSP returns an action chunk faster than any policy we compare. Compact, body-specific visual readouts also emerge without spatial supervision: manipulation commands depend strongly on task objects, while locomotion commands respond more broadly to the scene. On nine simulated Unitree G1 whole-body tasks, BSP matches the $Ψ_0$ humanoid foundation model with $75\times$ fewer parameters and nearly doubles Diffusion Policy's success. The same holds on a real G1 and a Fetch mobile manipulator.

items.title: Bridging institutional AI strategy and subject-level teaching practice: A school-level design framework for responsible AI-supported learning
items.abstract: The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has accelerated institutional investment in AI infrastructure, yet many universities continue to face difficulties translating institutional strategy into consistent subject-level teaching practice. This paper presents a School-level framework developed at an Australian university. The paper reports the design rationale, outputs and approved deployment model of the framework, including staff capability resources, configurable AI templates, disclosure mechanisms and governance processes. Informed by Educational Design Research and scholarship on organisational change in education, the paper argues that Schools can serve as meso-level environments that enact institutional AI strategy through resources and structures designed to support subject-level teaching practice. It contributes a meso-level governance model, six transferable design principles, and an operational framework intended to support responsible and human-centred AI-supported learning. Formal evaluation is planned following the pilot phase.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: Bridging the articulation gap: A multi-agent conversational AI platform for compassionate scaffolding of technical interview skills
items.abstract: Technical job interviews place computing students under pressure to demonstrate algorithmic and communication skills simultaneously under live observation, producing what we term the articulation gap. Existing preparation pathways provide only partial support: coding platforms ignore communication, coaching is economically inaccessible, and current AI simulators remain reactive. We present AIView, a multi-agent conversational platform that scaffolds integrated interview competencies. A LangGraph orchestrator coordinates specialised agents for question delivery and adaptive guidance alongside verbalisation monitors and an affect-aware tone layer, with assessments anchored in the SOLO taxonomy. An evaluation with 31 students showed high usability (SUS = 73.8), strong trust in AI feedback (M = 3.94), and high recommendation intent (M = 4.29). Participants valued personalised, code-aware feedback and a low-pressure learning environment. By fostering compassionate human-AI collaboration that supports creative problem solving and connection in a digital learning environment, AIView represents a step towards democratising access to career preparation through adaptive scaffolding.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: Building creativity with generative AI through reflective practice
items.abstract: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

items.title: Can Activation Steering Substitute for Prompt-Based Affective Priming in LLM Digital Twins?
items.abstract: Affective priming -- asking participants to write about a recalled event, such as a time they felt grateful or lacked control, and then measuring the induced state and its spillover onto related judgments -- is a standard way to manipulate emotion in the social sciences, and it also shifts the responses of LLM-based digital twins. The writing task, however, requires generating a full text. We test whether activation steering can replace it. Using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 100 personas in two domains (gratitude, lack of control), we compare a real-prompt path replicating the original Twin-2K-500 Mega Study (J2) with an injection path that skips the writing and adds a mean-difference direction, extracted from human writing, to the residual stream at varying strengths. The real-prompt effects fall between the original human and digital-twin effects in 5 of 6 comparisons. Injection shifts the manipulation check in a dose-dependent way and matches the real-prompt effect at one strength in the gratitude domain (beta ~ 2.7), but overshoots beyond it, on the proximal measure as well, and asymmetrically across the two directions. A structure-matched No-Injection baseline separates two sources of difference: omitting the writing task raises the proximal measure in both domains, whereas the injected direction itself moves a distal measure in the lack-of-control domain. Substitution is therefore measure-dependent: validity established for one way of inducing a state does not carry over uniformly to another.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Can GenAI numeracy tutors support self-regulated learning?
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: Can Vision-Language Models Truly Understand Images? A Benchmark Beyond Commonsense Bias
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks. However, it remains unclear whether their predictions are grounded in the visual content itself or are largely driven by statistical co-occurrence patterns and commonsense correlations learned from large-scale image-text corpora. Existing vision-language benchmarks predominantly consist of samples that conform to human commonsense, allowing models to achieve strong performance by exploiting dataset priors rather than genuinely understanding image content. To address this limitation, we present ContraSense, a systematically constructed benchmark for evaluating faithful vision-language understanding. ContraSense consists of carefully curated counter-intuitive image-text pairs that deliberately violate common expectations, substantially reducing the effectiveness of statistical biases and requiring models to rely on visual evidence for reasoning. We conduct comprehensive evaluations on a diverse set of representative open- and closed-source MLLMs. The results reveal a substantial performance gap between current MLLMs and humans: even the strongest closed-source model achieves only about 60\% accuracy, compared with 96.04\% for human participants. These findings demonstrate that current MLLMs still struggle with faithful visual understanding and highlight the need for more robust multimodal reasoning grounded in image content. The ContraSense benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingLin00/ContraSense.

items.title: Cartoon Motion Model
items.abstract: Generative 3D motion has shown impressive capabilities for authoring movements, but the integration into animation production is currently hindered by the discrepancy between realistic human motion capture and the exaggerated, non-physical movements of stylized animated feature characters. Nonetheless, hand-animated data is sparse, heterogeneous and incomplete, making it a challenging domain for data-hungry generative models. In this work, we introduce a framework that enables generation and control of stylized 3D motion by leveraging a pre-trained human motion prior. Our approach introduces robust data filtering techniques to handle inconsistent and noisy production movements. We train an unconditional ControlNet that eases adaptation by optimizing for maximum alignment between the motion capture and hand-animated domains. The generations of such model are also controllable through a spectral inpainting scheme that exposes parameters for exaggeration, source consistency and multi-character identities. We bridge the gap between physical conformity and artistic stylization and enable a diverse set of applications ranging from retargeting human performances to character-to-character motion transfer.

items.title: CATALOGAÇÃO ASSISTIDA POR INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL EM AMBIENTE REAL: EFICIÊNCIA, COMPLETUDE E SOBERANIA TÉCNICA DO BIBLIOTECÁRIO
items.abstract: Esta pesquisa analisou a incorporação de um módulo multimodal de inteligência artificial (IA), o Acelerador de Catalogação, a um sistema de gestão de bibliotecas, com objetivo central de considerar o impacto dessa ferramenta na rotina de processamento técnico, avaliando a eficiência operacional, a precisão da extração de dados e a facilidade de uso, com especial atenção à preservação da soberania técnica do bibliotecário. Realizou-se um estudo de caso quali-quantitativo em ambiente real de trabalho, com 12 bibliotecários voluntários experientes em catalogação tradicional. Os dados quantitativos, extraídos automaticamente pelo sistema, compararam 52 registros do regime tradicional e 64 do regime assistido por IA; os dados qualitativos vieram de um fórum de diálogo colaborativo, contido como ferramenta do próprio software com recursos de interação e engajamento, este fórum foi subdividido em cinco eixos temáticos, tratado por análise de conteúdo. Os resultados evidenciaram uma redução média por título que caiu 32,5% (de 10 min 13 s para 6 min 54 s) e a completude aumentou 24,5% (de 23,6 para 29,4 campos preenchidos). A IA foi eficaz em tarefas mimeomórficas (ações mecânicas, repetitivas e estruturadas), enquanto as tarefas polimórficas, que exigem julgamento contextual, tratamento de exceções e adequação a políticas locais, permaneceram com o profissional, porém com sugestões do agente de IA. Observou-se maior incidência de edições posteriores ao cadastro no regime assistido (11 em 64 processos, contra 2 em 52), concentrada em um catalogador e em obras jurídicas. Os participantes descreveram a tecnologia como “assistente sob comando”, o que sustenta a curadoria humana como componente estrutural do fluxo. Concluiu-se que o ganho de eficiência convive com a preservação da autoridade técnica e do protagonismo do bibliotecário.

items.title: Caught in the algorithm: Student discourse on AI governance, surveillance, and academic integrity in higher education
items.abstract: This study examines how awareness of generative AI academic integrity policies shapes student anxiety, ethical reasoning, and writing practices in higher education. Drawing on a reflexive thematic analysis of student discourse from YouTube and Reddit, the study explores how detection-oriented governance frameworks are experienced and negotiated outside formal institutional contexts. Findings indicate that students do not primarily describe intentional rule-breaking; instead, they articulate experiences of surveillance, uncertainty, and adaptation within assessment systems perceived as inconsistent and adversarial. Three interrelated themes are identified: surveillance anxiety and defensive authorship; normative dissonance and moral negotiation of AI use; and cognitive offloading, systemic strain, and declining trust in assessment integrity. Across these themes, AI policy awareness is shown to shape not only behavioural responses but also students’ affective and epistemic relationships with writing, authorship, and institutional authority. The study argues that detection-first approaches risk intensifying anxiety and undermining trust without resolving underlying tensions in assessment design. It concludes that generative AI exposes structural fragilities in higher education, suggesting the need to reorient academic integrity governance toward design-led, transparent, and equity-sensitive approaches that prioritise learning, trust, and student experience.

items.title: Characterising human cognitive security and its behavioural outcomes within an integrative modelling framework
items.abstract: Human decision-making under uncertainty faces growing challenges from information-based threats that pose risks to human cognitive processes and behaviour. Although their potential harm is widely acknowledged, there remains no well-defined construct for characterising the degree to which information-based threats influence changes in human judgments and decision-making, impeding theoretical advancement, measurement, and effective countermeasure development. Here, we introduce a human cognitive security construct focused on linking information-based threats to observable outcomes to bridge field-level definitions with operational measures by drawing from core mechanisms related to information processing and decision-making. To connect the information environment to behaviour, we develop an integrative modelling framework that unifies Bayesian inference with affect-modulated decision valuation, capturing how cognitive resource allocation and affective valuation shape three core behavioural outcomes: veracity discernment, task-oriented actions, and information sharing. Through computational simulations, we demonstrate that this framework can explain canonical phenomena, including cognitive heuristics and incongruent veracity discernment and sharing behaviour, and we test model predictions against empirical data of the illusory truth effect (R² = 0.86). To guide future empirical examinations, we propose empirically grounded behavioural outcome measures of cognitive security and outline how environment-specific elements, characterised by data availability and ecological constraints, affect individuals’ cognitive security.

items.title: Classification AI vs Generative AI in grading and feedback
items.abstract: Marking is among the most time-consuming activities in education, and artificial intelligence (AI) is widely proposed as a remedy. Attention has centred on generative large language models, yet regulators raise concerns about their bias, consistency, and explainability. This paper contrasts generative grading with per-question classification models trained only on an educator’s own marking and deployed in a human-in-the-loop workflow. The architectures are compared against criteria drawn from regulatory guidance: transparency, construct-relevant features, determinism, and specifiable training data. A narrower role for generative models is also identified, in composing and restructuring marker-approved feedback rather than in marking. Deployment analytics from one platform are then reported, covering approximately 166,000 marked questions, 39,500 essays, and six institutions: 66.2% of questions were marked in under one minute, 77.6% to 89.5% of AI suggestions were accepted, and essay models reached a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.93 for high-confidence predictions. Questionnaire responses from earlier pilots (33 markers, 30 students) are also reported: markers described marking as faster and consistent feedback as easier to provide; most students rated feedback more consistent and higher in quality. Implications for institutions selecting or building such tools are discussed, alongside the limitations of vendor-collected data.

items.title: Client Perceptions of the Quality of the Occupational Health Physiotherapy Service
items.abstract: Background: Occupational health physiotherapy supports workforce resilience and return-to-work outcomes. Evaluating client perceptions of service quality offers critical insight into therapeutic alliance and client focussed care. This project evaluated client perceptions of the quality of an occupational health physiotherapy service to identify key strengths and areas for improvement. Methods: Over six months, clients attending the service completed the validated SERVQUAL questionnaire at discharge. The survey evaluated five core dimensions: tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, and empathy. The attending physiotherapist captured demographic, work, and health data. Descriptive statistics summarised client characteristics, importance ratings, and satisfaction across job roles. Results: Fifty-five questionnaires were analysed (mean age: 43.2 years; 80% female). Most clients were actively working (89.1%), presenting primarily with spinal conditions (47.3%). Medical and clinical staff comprised the largest user group (61.8%). Responsiveness (94.5%) and empathy (92.7%) were rated highest in importance, followed by reliability (90.1%), assurance (89.1%), and tangibles (69.1%). Service quality scores was highest in interpersonal dimensions, with administrative and support staff reporting near-unanimous positive evaluations. However, tangibles received the lowest service quality score and the most neutral responses. Conclusion: The service excels in relational care, empathy, and operational dependability, effectively fostering therapeutic trust and workforce retention. To align the physical clinical environment with its high standard of clinical excellence, targeted investment in upgrading clinic facilities and equipment (i.e., tangibles) is recommended.

items.title: Clinician Acceptance of Large Language Model–Generated Discharge Summaries
items.abstract: Importance: Hospital discharge summaries are essential for continuity of care, but fragmented electronic health record (EHR) data can compromise their quality and safety. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for clinical documentation tasks despite limited evidence regarding their performance in health care settings compared with the current standard of care. Objective: To evaluate clinician acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries derived from EHRs compared with routine clinician-written summaries. Design, Setting, and Participants: In this retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework, acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries was compared with clinician-authored discharge summaries. Admission records from 5 London hospitals for September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, were evaluated against the full admission record by practicing physicians. Admissions were eligible only if the clinician-authored discharge summary contained identifiable clinical summary, plan and requested actions, and information given sections. Data analysis was conducted from July 2025 to February 2026. Intervention: LLM-generated summaries were produced using GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI) and a clinician-codesigned prompt. Main Outcomes and Measures: The primary outcome was clinician signoff with no or minor edits, derived from 2 sequential questions: (1) whether the reviewer would sign the summary and (2) whether no, minor, or major edits were required. A 5-percentage-point noninferiority margin was prespecified. Secondary outcomes assessed accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, poor; 2, fair; 3, good; 4, very good; and 5, excellent) and potential harmfulness of missing or incorrect information (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, no harm; 2, minor harm; 3, moderate harm; 4, high harm; and 5, extremely high harm). Results: The study sample included 1294 (649 clinician-authored and 645 LLM-generated) unique case discharge summaries that were evaluated against the full admission record by 12 practicing physicians. Case patients had a median age of 46.0 years (IQR, 26.2-69.8 years), 733 (56.6%) were assigned female at birth, and the median length of stay was 3.0 days (IQR, 1.0-7.0 days). The absolute difference in model-estimated probability of signoff with no or minor edits (LLM generated minus clinician authored) was 22.2 percentage points (95% CI, 19.0-27.5 percentage points); the lower bound exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of -5 percentage points, demonstrating noninferiority. LLM-generated summaries received higher ratings for accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (adjusted risk differences for scores ≥4 ranged from 19.4 [95% CI, 14.8-24.1] to 29.1 [95% CI, 25.1-33.6] percentage points; all 95% CIs excluded 0). LLM-generated summaries also had a lower proportion of cases rated 3 or greater for potential harm on the clinical summary and plan and requested actions sections (140 of 534 [26.2%] and 124 of 462 [26.8%]) compared with clinician-authored summaries (271 of 601 [45.1%] and 278 of 540 [51.5%]). Conclusions and Relevance: In this study, LLM-generated discharge summaries met the current standard of care, representing a promising early use case for generative artificial intelligence in health care with close clinician oversight.

items.title: Cluster-Guided Decoding with Trust-Region Constraints for Personalized Recommendation
items.abstract: Most recommenders score each item in the catalog separately, and do not explicitly model which semantic region of the catalog a recommendation belongs to. Models expressive enough to offer that control are often too slow to run over a full catalog for online inference. In this paper, we present Cluster-Guided Generative Reconstruction (CG2R), which learns a hierarchy of semantic clusters and uses a cluster-level prior to steer item ranking for personalized recommendations. Unlike existing systems that only use clusters to pre-select candidates, CG2R adds the cluster prior directly to the item scoring rule, so that the learned cluster structure shapes the ranking itself. Because the prior is assembled from cluster centroids rather than per-item statistics, it remains defined even for cold-start users when no history is available. Across the three benchmark datasets evaluated, CG2R outperforms classical, neural, and LLM-based baselines in terms of Recall and nDCG, with its performance gains widening as the catalog grows sparser. In addition, CG2R serves recommendations in milliseconds, suggesting potential as low-latency first-stage retrieval.

items.title: Cogniti agents in practice: AI as academic infrastructure in a foundation business course
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering universities not only as a student-owned productivity tool but as part of the digital infrastructure through which learning support, feedback and assessment guidance are mediated. This concise paper reports on an exploratory pilot of Cogniti AI agents in an Aotearoa New Zealand foundation business course, with a focus on human-centred learning design. The pilot involved five role-specialised agents: a course buddy for administration support, a case-discussion agent for Maori entrepreneurship learning, and three virtual team members focused on task coordination, relationship management and value-adding contribution. Rather than positioning AI as a generic chatbot, the paper presents a design model for embedding AI agents within the course ecosystem. Drawing on design records, early usage patterns and practice reflections, the paper argues that AI agents can extend human-centred pedagogy when they are co-created with students, shaped by student input, assessment-aligned, and circumscribed by teacher oversight. The contribution is a practical model for integrating AI agents into learning management systems in ways that prioritise connection, mentorship, evaluative judgement, feedback literacy and collaborative learning.

items.title: Combining structural equation modeling, necessary condition analysis and explainable machine learning reveals distinct drivers and preconditions of student ChatGPT adoption
items.abstract: Universities need to know which factors raise students’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence and which must be present before high intention can occur. The hybrid structural equation and neural network analyses that dominate this literature address only the first question, rank predictors with a heuristic importance index and rarely test prediction on new respondents. We re-analyzed an open survey of 1,242 ChatGPT-using university students from 78 Philippine institutions, combining partial least squares structural equation modeling, necessary condition analysis, gradient boosting explained with Shapley values and cross-validated predictive tests. Habit was the strongest unique predictor of intention to use ChatGPT yet ranked sixth or seventh of seven on necessity under every scoring, whereas effort expectancy, with no detectable unique effect, ranked among the top three. Necessity magnitudes depended on the Likert response distributions and fell below conventional thresholds after rank transformation, so the robust result is this inverted ordering rather than the magnitudes. The three importance rankings agreed at the top and bottom, and neither the structural model nor the boosted ensemble predicted new respondents better than a linear benchmark. Separating predictors that raise intention from those that must be present gives institutions a clearer basis for sequencing support.

items.title: Comparative Ergonomic Assessment of Microscopic, Endoscopic, and RobOtol®-Assisted Ear Surgery: A Prospective Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background: Otologic surgery imposes prolonged static postures and fine-motor demands on the surgeon, yet the ergonomic effect of robotic endoscope holding is unknown. We compared surgeon-perceived workload, fatigue and workflow during microscopic, conventional endoscopic and RobOtol®-assisted endoscopic ear surgery. Methods: In this prospective single-center pilot study, one surgeon performed 29 procedures: RobOtol® (n = 9), conventional endoscopy (n = 10) and microscopy (n = 10). After each procedure, the surgeon rated five NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX)-derived workload domains (0–10; unweighted mean), comfort, neck, eye and hand fatigue, instrument stability and movement precision. Setup time, operative time and repositionings were recorded. Kruskal–Wallis and Holm-adjusted Mann–Whitney U tests were used, with false discovery rate control across secondary outcomes. Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) scores from intraoperative photographs were analyzed descriptively. Results: Modified NASA-TLX scores were 3.58 ± 1.50 (RobOtol®), 3.78 ± 1.54 (endoscopy) and 5.52 ± 1.54 (microscopy) (p = 0.026, ε2 = 0.26); no pairwise difference remained significant after Holm adjustment. Eye fatigue was higher with microscopy than with either endoscopic approach (adjusted p ≤ 0.016). Compared with conventional endoscopy, RobOtol® yielded higher surgeon-rated instrument stability (mean difference 2.72, 95% CI 1.79–3.65; adjusted p < 0.001) and movement precision (1.04, 95% CI 0.41–1.67; adjusted p = 0.019) without higher workload. Operative time was longest with microscopy (130.7 vs 76.8 and 77.3 min; p = 0.004). Mean RULA scores were 3.38–3.77 (action level 2) in all groups. Conclusions: Endoscopic approaches were associated with lower perceived workload and eye fatigue than microscopy, and robotic endoscope holding was associated with higher perceived stability and precision without added workload. As case mix differed between groups and outcomes were self-rated, these hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in larger multi-surgeon studies with objective performance and posture measurement.

items.title: Comparing Implicit and Explicit Language Attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal in Humans and Large Language Models
items.abstract: While language attitudes have been extensively studied in humans, the extent to which large language models (LLMs) encode similar associations between language varieties and social attributes remains unclear. Contemporary sociolinguistic research distinguishes between explicit attitudes, which stem from deliberative processing, and implicit attitudes, which arise from automatic processing. This study investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like implicit and explicit language attitudes toward the Dutch multiethnolect Straattaal, particularly its association with migrant communities. We use closely matched designs to assess attitudes in humans and LLMs. For humans, we use an Implicit Association Test (IAT) and an explicit rating task. For LLMs, we use the LLM Word Association Test (LLM WAT) and the same explicit rating task. Human participants strongly associate Straattaal with individuals with a migration background at both implicit and explicit levels. In the LLM WAT, Straattaal is consistently associated with individuals with a migration background, with stronger associations observed in larger and newer models. When presented with the same explicit rating task as human participants, LLMs produce comparable response patterns. Overall, the findings suggest that many LLMs encode language attitudes resembling those observed in humans, however we also highlight important questions about how concepts and measures developed to study human attitudes should be interpreted in LLMs. This highlights the relevance of incorporating sociolinguistic perspectives and language variation into NLP research to better identify and mitigate socially and linguistically embedded biases.

items.title: Comparing the positive and negative impacts of AI: A large-scale study of student perspectives
items.abstract: Higher education students are incorporating generative artificial intelligence into many aspects of their studies, yet the ways they judge its positive and negative impacts remain poorly understood. Using qualitative content analysis supported by code-frequency analysis, this paper examines open-ended comments from 2,802 participants drawn from a survey of 8,021 students across four Australian universities. Reported impacts clustered around four themes: study practices, quality, efficiency, and institutional practices. Positive impacts were more frequently coded overall, particularly when students described using AI to support their own study practices and efficiency. Negative responses centred on the inaccuracy of AI outputs. Although relatively few participants commented on institutional teaching and assessment practices, these responses were predominantly negative. The findings suggest that students value AI not only for the quality of its outputs, but also for its role in helping them begin, continue, refine, and complete academic work. Rather than uncritically accepting or categorically rejecting AI, students appeared to make situated judgements about its usefulness and limitations, shaped by concerns about accuracy and trust, as well as by the agency and control they retained over its use. Institutional responses should therefore engage with the complexity of students’ practices and the conditions under which they perceive AI to be useful or problematic.

items.title: Compassionate AI by design: Reconnecting students with learning through course-tailored AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of students’ everyday study practices, yet institutional debate still tends to position it as either an efficiency tool or an academic-integrity threat. This binary framing obscures a more educationally useful question: can AI be designed to help students engage meaningfully with difficult concepts while helping educators see where understanding breaks down? This project evaluates a course-tailored AI learning assistant embedded in a large undergraduate course at an Australian public university. The tool was bounded to authoritative course materials and instructor-provided resources. Students could ask questions, receive course-grounded answers and explanations, and clarify or organise their understanding without having assessed tasks completed for them. Informed by self-determination theory and cognitive load theory, the design sought to support competence and autonomy, reduce unnecessary cognitive burden, and provide low-stakes help at the moment of uncertainty (Ryan & Deci, 2000; Sweller, 1988). Students were randomly assigned either access to the tool or standard course resources. Evaluation drew on complementary sources of evidence gathered across the teaching period, combining students’ own accounts of their experience with routinely captured indicators of engagement and achievement. The evidence points in a consistent direction. Students with access reported a more positive orientation towards their study and towards the responsible institutional use of AI. Their engagement shifted in character rather than in volume, suggesting sustained attention to core course materials rather than a general increase in undifferentiated digital activity. Indications for achievement were encouraging, particularly for students at greater risk of not succeeding, although the strength of these signals varied. An equally important feature lay in the questions themselves. Patterns in students’ questions made recurring misconceptions and points of uncertainty more visible to the educator. This supported more responsive teaching: explanations, examples, and follow-up support could be focused on what students were actually struggling to understand. The initiative therefore created a two-way pedagogical feedback loop. Students received immediate, course-aligned support for working through concepts, while the educator gained diagnostic insight into learning needs not always visible in conventional analytics or classroom participation. The project locates compassion in the design choices, not in the technology itself. Course alignment, bounded assistance, student choice, and attention to digital burden offer a way for AI to support conceptual engagement without displacing core resources or student agency (Burr et al., 2020; Holmes et al., 2022). The resulting principles are to ground AI in authoritative course materials, preserve the integrity of assessed work, enable low-stakes questioning, use question patterns to inform teaching, and evaluate wellbeing alongside engagement and achievement. These principles are applicable across disciplines and tertiary contexts.

items.title: Computer-Gamified Pedagogy in English Vocabulary Teaching
items.abstract: To address the problems of decontextualized vocabulary drills and the lack of adaptive, data-informed instruction, this study designs and evaluates a web-based gamified vocabulary system integrating an adaptive task sequencing algorithm, real-time learning analytics, and multimodal scenarios within a constructivist framework. In a 16-week quasi-experiment with 200 non-English-major undergraduates, the experimental group (n = 100) improved by 22.5 points in total vocabulary score, in comparison with an improvement of 11.3 points in the control group (n = 100), with the largest gains made in low-frequency word mastery (+41.5%) and vocabulary application (+39.6%). The experimental group also reported higher intrinsic motivation (4.32 vs. 3.56, p < .001), and platform logs showed task completion rising from 78.6% to 93.8% and error rate falling from 28.4% to 10.1%. Two teachers used the dashboard for data-informed instructional adjustments. These findings illustrate how web-based learning technologies can support learner autonomy and instructional decision-making in higher education.

items.title: Computing Conditional Shapley Values Using Tabular Foundation Models
items.abstract: Shapley values have become a cornerstone of explainable AI, but they are computationally expensive to use, especially when features are dependent. Evaluating them requires approximating a large number of conditional expectations, either via Monte Carlo integration or regression. Until recently it has not been possible to fully exploit deep learning for the regression approach, because retraining for each conditional expectation takes too long. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN overcome this computational hurdle by leveraging in-context learning, so each conditional expectation can be approximated without any re-training. In this paper, we compute Shapley values with multiple variants of TabPFN and compare their performance with state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real datasets. In most cases, TabPFN yields the best performance; where it does not, it is only marginally worse than the best method, at a fraction of the runtime. We discuss further improvements and how tabular foundation models can be better adapted specifically for conditional Shapley value estimation.

items.title: Concisely Explaining the Doubt: Minimum-Size Abductive Explanations for Linear Models with a Reject Option
items.abstract: Trustworthiness in artificial intelligence depends not only on what a model decides, but also on how it handles and explains cases in which a reliable decision cannot be made. In critical domains such as healthcare and finance, a reject option allows the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient, making it essential to explain why an instance is rejected in order to support informed human intervention. In these settings, explanations must not only be interpretable, but also faithful to the underlying model and computationally efficient enough to support real-time decision making. Abductive explanations guarantee fidelity, but their exact computation is known to be NP-hard for many classes of models, limiting their practical applicability. Computing minimum-size abductive explanations is an even more challenging problem, as it requires reasoning not only about fidelity but also about optimality. Prior work has addressed this challenge in restricted settings, including log-linear-time algorithms for computing minimum-size abductive explanations in linear models without rejection, as well as a polynomial-time method based on linear programming for computing abductive explanations, without guarantees of minimum size, for linear models with a reject option. In this work, we bridge these lines of research by computing minimum-size abductive explanations for linear models with a reject option. For accepted instances, we adapt the log-linear algorithm to efficiently compute optimal explanations. For rejected instances, we formulate a 0–1 integer linear programming problem that characterizes minimum-size abductive explanations of rejection. Although this formulation is NP-hard in theory, our experimental results show that it is consistently more efficient in practice than the linear-programming-based approach that does not guarantee minimum-size explanations.

items.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
items.abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.

items.title: Content licensing strategy in AI–publisher coopetition: the role of asymmetric comparative advantages and citation intensity
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

items.title: Context Matters for Tech Use and Development
items.abstract: This chapter examines everyday digital practices on the Cape Flats. Through ethnographic engagement with residents and tech entrepreneurs, we demonstrate how context matters in understanding the importance of the phone as critical social infrastructure amid poverty, violence, and uneven connectivity. We ask whose rights to connectivity, privacy, and transparency in data collection are considered. The chapter analyzes barriers to access in the digital economy and why developing tech from the Cape Flats matters in breaking stereotypes about people from the area. We consider much-needed initiatives in terms of solving local problems with tech, while querying the awkward promises of the Silicon Cape, situating findings within broader debates on sociotechnical imaginaries, classification, and algorithmic bias. We argue that understanding tech and energy futures requires sustained attention to context, place-based inequality, racialization, and historical dispossession. Data is the business model for tech startups and tech giants alike. With a mobile phone in the pocket and across “smart technologies,” data is generated, stored, and shared—often in opaque ways—as the commodification of everyday interactions turns life into data. We ground this discussion and consider the everyday realities and material conditions that tech responds to—solving or augmenting the issues depending on viewpoint.

items.title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates
items.abstract: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.

items.title: Controlling Proactive Multimodal AI: Separating Perception from Participation
items.abstract: Proactive multimodal AI can watch a user's screen, listen to speech, track interaction, and decide whether to enter unfolding work. Little is known about how people want to control what such AI may perceive and how far it may participate. Informed by a 14-person Wizard-of-Oz study, we built SpotMe, a design probe that senses screen, speech, and interaction; chooses Silence, Ask, or Assist; and lets users separately configure what it may perceive, how far it may participate, and what types of support it may provide. In a 16-person study on a civic dashboard, participants first experienced proactive help, then inspected decisions to act or remain silent, and then configured SpotMe's perception and participation. We found that participants could keep all perception channels available while lowering participation to Ask or Silence; that exposing suppressed decisions made silence interpretable and contestable; and that seeing what SpotMe used led some to change how they clicked, highlighted, and spoke. We contribute an empirical account of inspecting and controlling proactive multimodal AI by decoupling perception from participation.

items.title: Conversational pedagogy in practice: Exploring a unit-embedded GenAI chatbot in higher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are increasingly being adopted in higher education; however, limited research has examined their pedagogical integration within learning environments. This paper reports findings from an exploratory mixed-methods case study of a GenAI chatbot embedded in a postgraduate unit at an Australian university. Designed as a pedagogically embedded learning companion, the chatbot provided contextualised guidance and functioned as a first point of contact for students seeking clarification and support. Findings indicate that students perceived the chatbot as a useful and accessible learning resource that supported engagement, reflection, and self-directed learning. Three themes emerged: first-contact pedagogical support, AI-mediated scaffolding, and human-AI complementarity. Students valued the immediacy and contextual relevance of responses while recognising the continuing importance of educator guidance. These initial findings provide insights into the design of pedagogically embedded GenAI learning companions and their potential role in supporting learning within higher education.

items.title: Cross-attention Guided CNN-Transformer-GNN Architecture for Multi-class Disaster Image Classification
items.abstract: Disaster image classification emerged as an important research area for supporting rapid disaster assessment, situational awareness, and emergency response operations.Nevertheless, accurately distinguishing among different disaster categories remains challenging due to large intra-class variations, complex backgrounds, and the limited capability of existing approaches to simultaneously capture local visual patterns, global contextual dependencies, and inter-feature relationships.To tackle these challenges, this study proposes a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-Transformer-Graph Neural Network (GNN) approach incorporating a Cross-Attention Gating Block (CAGB) for multi-class disaster image classification.The proposed architecture combines InceptionV3-based convolutional feature extraction with Transformer-based contextual representation learning and Lightweight GNN-based relational feature modeling to generate comprehensive feature representations.Furthermore, the CAGB adaptively refines and integrates heterogeneous features through cross-attention-guided gating, enabling enhanced discrimination among disaster categories.The proposed framework was assessed on a disaster image dataset comprising Cyclone, Earthquake, Flood, and Wildfire classes with 4,428 images.Experimental results demonstrated classification performance, attaining an accuracy of 96.16%, macro-average precision of 96.33%, macro-average recall of 96.10%, macro-average F1-score of 96.20%, and micro-average ROC-AUC of 99.71%.Comparative analysis with existing disaster image classification methods further verified the effectiveness of the proposed approach, highlighting its potential for intelligent disaster monitoring and decision-support applications.

items.title: Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo
items.abstract: Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

items.title: CustomDance: Customized 3D Dance Generation with Coarse-to-Fine Human-Centered Interactive Control
items.abstract: With the rise of AI-generated content (AIGC) and advanced techniques for 3D human representation, the task of generating 3D dance movements has become an exciting area of research. Despite significant advancements, current methods often fail to provide comprehensive and distinct control over various multimodal inputs from users, such as music or specific descriptions of desired movements. As a result, the generated motions may be statistically plausible and technically correct, but they often lack depth, expressiveness, and alignment with the user’s creative vision. To address this issue, we present CustomDance, a coarse-to-fine interactive system designed for customized 3D dance generation. Inspired by the workflows of expert choreographers, CustomDance introduces a novel paradigm to AI-assisted choreography through three interconnected stages. First, a multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) analyzes the music and a high-level text prompt to identify key temporal anchors and creative cues for the piece. Next, for each anchor, a multimodal retriever suggests high-quality motion clips from a dance library based on local music and text, empowering the user with concrete and predictable options. Finally, a custom music-conditioned diffusion in-painter seamlessly connects the selected phrases, allowing for iterative, user-guided refinement of the final composition, supported by visualizations of motion dynamics. Our evaluations demonstrate that CustomDance not only highlights the significant creative utility and empowering potential of our AI-assisted choreography paradigm, but also outperforms competitive baselines across quantitative and qualitative comparisons. items.title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
items.abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

items.title: DailyBrick: Language-Guided Synthesis of Brick Assembly Instructions
items.abstract: Generating a LEGO model from a user request is more than a plausible 3D shape generation. LEGO models require physical support per brick, and each brick should be placed unblocked. Current methods address this issue by training an expert large language model. We reduce the problem of generating extremely long context on all brick connections to that of writing a program that builds LEGO models like a human, considering each intermediate step could be executed. We introduce DailyBrick , a multi-stage agentic system that produces a LEGO model together with a brick-by-brick assembly instruction for human building and robot assembly. We design a multi-stage harness with roles to help LLMs generate more effectively. A versioned construction SDK compiles multi-level decisions, from semantic subparts to individual bricks, into canonical operations. An external Meta-Reviewer agent replays and inspects the generated package, verifies the model and its construction process, identifies failures, traces them to the responsible stage, and routes them to bounded repairs or to editable candidates for later skill or tool updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DailyBrick generates LEGO models based on simple user requests better than recent agentic systems, and show its utility in downstream applications such as robot manipulations on model assembly from instructions and brick sets (https://spatialagentlab.github.io/DailyBrick.github.io/).

items.title: Decoupling Identity and Agency: A Comparative Public International Law Framework on AI Impersonation and Human Rights
items.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and zero-shot biometric synthesis has engineered an ontological decoupling of human identity from physical agency. High-fidelity synthetic media—or "deepfakes"—can now instantaneously weaponise minor biometric samples, outpacing both organic human perception and traditional algorithmic forensic detection. This paper provides an exhaustive comparative and doctrinal critique of the highly fragmented legal architectures racing to govern malicious synthetic impersonation. First, it interrogates the acute constitutional friction within the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), balancing the protection of individual dignity and image rights under Article 8 against protected artistic and political expression under Article 10. Second, it establishes a comparative matrix contrasting the disparate paradigms enacted globally: the European Union's focus on systemic platform-level risk and technological transparency; the United States' property-centric reliance on commercial publicity rights tethered by fierce First Amendment protections; the United Kingdom's patchwork of legacy common law torts stretched to address modern digital harm; and China's prescriptive model of upstream authoritarian control. Finally, this article confronts the catastrophic breakdown of Public International Law (PIL) mechanisms regarding cross-border enforcement, conflict of laws, and state attribution rules under Article 8 of the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA). Because post-hoc detection capabilities face imminent collapse, this paper argues that the international community must move beyond domestic fragmentation to codify a universal treaty-based "Digital Right to Identity" reinforced by mandatory, hardware-level cryptographic provenance.

items.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and zero-shot biometric synthesis has engineered an ontological decoupling of human identity from physical agency. High-fidelity synthetic media—or "deepfakes"—can now instantaneously weaponise minor biometric samples, outpacing both organic human perception and traditional algorithmic forensic detection. This paper provides an exhaustive comparative and doctrinal critique of the highly fragmented legal architectures racing to govern malicious synthetic impersonation. First, it interrogates the acute constitutional friction within the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), balancing the protection of individual dignity and image rights under Article 8 against protected artistic and political expression under Article 10. Second, it establishes a comparative matrix contrasting the disparate paradigms enacted globally: the European Union's focus on systemic platform-level risk and technological transparency; the United States' property-centric reliance on commercial publicity rights tethered by fierce First Amendment protections; the United Kingdom's patchwork of legacy common law torts stretched to address modern digital harm; and China's prescriptive model of upstream authoritarian control. Finally, this article confronts the catastrophic breakdown of Public International Law (PIL) mechanisms regarding cross-border enforcement, conflict of laws, and state attribution rules under Article 8 of the Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA). Because post-hoc detection capabilities face imminent collapse, this paper argues that the international community must move beyond domestic fragmentation to codify a universal treaty-based "Digital Right to Identity" reinforced by mandatory, hardware-level cryptographic provenance.

items.title: Designing AI-mediated interactive learning environments for communication skills: Insights from two implementations
items.abstract: Developing communication skills remains a core challenge in higher education, particularly in providing scalable opportunities for practice and feedback. This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated systems function as interactive learning environments for communication skills development. Two implementations are examined: a voice-only conversational AI-mediated system used across health disciplines and a digital human avatar used in a business unit. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative survey data and qualitative content. Findings highlighted three key affordances: repeated low-stakes practice, immediate feedback, and flexible engagement. Students reported increased confidence and perceived skill development. Limitations included conversational inaccuracies, realism, technical reliability, and feedback consistency. Importantly, findings indicate that the effectiveness of AI systems is strongly influenced by prompt design, scenario construction, and alignment with learner level. This paper reframes AI tools not as autonomous technologies, but as designed interactive learning environments requiring careful pedagogical integration. Implications are discussed for the design of AI-supported learning activities, particularly in contexts involving oral communication and authentic assessment.

items.title: Designing assessment through transformation: A learning beyond the classroom approach to AI-mediated assessment
items.abstract: Where does meaningful learning begin in an era of generative artificial intelligence (AI)? Current responses to AI in higher education have largely focused on assessment redesign, academic integrity and AI literacy. While these developments have strengthened assessment practice, they often assume that meaningful learning begins when students enter university. This paper argues that responding effectively to AI requires reconsidering this assumption. Drawing upon the learning beyond the classroom framework, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy for assessment design that recognises learners’ existing educational resources and supports their development into disciplinary judgement. This paper contributes in three ways. First, it introduces the learning beyond the classroom framework as a conceptual foundation for understanding learning in AI-mediated higher education. Second, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy that connects recognition, translation, transformation and disciplinary judgement within a developmental approach to assessment design. Third, it translates this philosophy into five practical principles that provide educators with a flexible lens for redesigning assessment across diverse disciplinary contexts. Rather than treating AI as the central educational challenge, the paper positions it as a catalyst for reconsidering the purposes of assessment, arguing that higher education’s enduring contribution lies in cultivating critical judgement, ethical reasoning and meaningful contribution.

items.title: Designing authentic learning through anchor scenarios: A whole-of-unit approach
items.abstract: In technology disciplines, students are more engaged and better prepared for employment when they experience technical work as purposeful professional practice rather than as isolated exercises (Kerven et al., 2017). Generative AI can now produce working code, configured systems and polished documentation, so students can complete tasks that mainly ask for these outputs without doing much of the work themselves. Such tasks are unlikely to hold students’ interest, and the work submitted can be weak evidence of capability. The professional judgement remains theirs: deciding what should be built, for whom, within which constraints, and with what consequences. The challenge for curriculum design is to integrate, teach and assess that judgement. This presentation describes a curriculum design we developed in response. Each unit is set in one authentic workplace context, the anchor scenario, which defines the stakeholders, constraints and outcome for the whole unit. Every session then presents a session scenario: a professional decision in that context, building on the one before. In the final assessment, students deliver the outcome the anchor scenario set. Content is taught when students need it for a decision, and assessment is set in the same context. The approach draws on situated learning, in which judgement develops through authentic activity in realistic contexts (Brown et al., 1989; Lave & Wenger, 1991), and on Action Mapping, which begins from a real workplace outcome and derives the decisions learners must make before selecting content (Moore, 2017). Narrative carries more force when scenarios accumulate rather than stand alone (Bruner, 1991). Sustained scenario structures have precedents: anchored instruction centres on one extended problem (Cognition and Technology Group at Vanderbilt, 1990), media computation organises content coverage (Guzdial, 2003), and task-driven case studies guide practice rather than judgement (Porubän et al., 2024). None spans an entire unit while structuring cumulative professional decisions, producing employer-facing artefacts, and giving AI a purposeful role. Each unit is built in three phases. The Anchor phase derives the scenario from a workplace outcome and produces a unit design plan mapping outcomes to assessments and giving every session its own scenario. The Embed phase scripts each session in full, writing assessments at the same time and checking alignment in both directions (Biggs, 1996), with every activity carrying a short connection back to the scenario. The Shift phase builds the design as web-based learning paths for delivery on campus, online or in hybrid mode. This approach now runs in more than 30 units across five discipline areas. They include a café point-of-sale system built over 11 programming sessions, a hospital network designed for a computer networking unit, and a robotic warehouse floor for an electrical engineering unit. The presentation walks through the designs themselves, alongside feedback from the teaching staff who delivered them. While the scenarios are varied, each design begins with the professional world and its people, derives the decisions from them, and lets the technology find its place inside that world.

items.title: Designing human-AI creative learning: A scoping review towards a human-centred framework for AI-assisted creativity in higher education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education by reshaping how learners generate ideas, solve problems, and engage in creative knowledge construction. While existing research has primarily examined the effectiveness of AI tools on learning outcomes, writing performance, and student engagement, comparatively little attention has been paid to understanding how educators intentionally design AI-assisted creative learning experiences. This paper presents a scoping review of 49 empirical and conceptual sources on AI-assisted creativity in higher education to identify recurring instructional design practices, human–AI interaction patterns, and pedagogical strategies. Rather than focusing on technological capabilities alone, the review synthesizes how creative learning activities are structured around collaboration between learners, educators, and AI systems, while also engaging directly with mixed evidence on AI’s creative value, including findings that AI-assisted ideation can expand idea novelty under some conditions, yet produce design fixation and narrowed divergent thinking under others. Building upon this synthesis, the paper proposes a preliminary Human-Centered AI Creativity Design (HACD) framework that positions AI as a collaborative creative partner while preserving learner agency, critical reflection, and ethical decision-making. The framework offers an initial conceptual model to guide educators in designing meaningful AI-supported creative learning experiences and provides a foundation for empirical validation.

items.title: Designing inclusive interactive oral assessments: Practical learnings for educators
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence continues to impact the higher education sector, Interactive Oral Assessments (IOAs) are increasingly used to assure assessment integrity. Whilst there are IOA best practice guidelines, there are concerns that the pace of implementation has compromised design, and considerations regarding student preparation, equity and inclusivity are being overlooked. This concise paper considers these issues through a case study of a postgraduate business subject and provides practical advice for how student preparation for oral tasks can be embedded within a curriculum without detracting from disciplinary knowledge and content. The design addressed five areas to support student IOA preparation: creating authentic scenarios; designing inclusive assessment practices for diverse cohorts; structured student preparation; balancing IOA preparation with course content coverage; and ensuring alignment between preparation activities and the actual IOA experience. Student feedback and educator observations suggest students felt increasingly prepared and supported throughout the semester. Recommendations are made for educators considering IOA including incorporation of low-stakes practice, creating classroom safety, setting clear expectations, preparing exemplars, focusing on student and educator preparation, and collaborating with others. This paper extends existing IOA literature by addressing inclusive practices for increasingly diverse student cohorts and contributes practical strategies for educators seeking to design IOA’s that support inclusion while balancing curriculum time and disciplinary content requirements.

items.title: Designing psychiatric environments tailored to the needs of geriatric patients: spatial solutions in geriatric hospital wards that reduce stress and dissorientation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The progressive aging of the population increases the demand for specialized psychiatric wards adapted to the needs of older adults. A particular challenge is designing spaces for patients with dementia, as environmental changes may cause disorientation, deterioration of mental condition, and increased behavioral disturbances. Properly designed therapeutic environments improve safety, support spatial orientation, and enhance psychological comfort. The aim of this study was to identify and analyze good design practices in geriatric psychiatric wards based on the principles of health-promoting architecture. MATERIAL AND METHODS: A narrative literature review was conducted, covering publications on healthcare architecture, environmental psychiatry, and therapeutic environment design, with particular focus on patients with dementia. Current guidelines, design recommendations, and practical solutions used in healthcare facilities were also analyzed. The study had a descriptive and comparative character. Identified architectural solutions were assessed using a qualitative comparative approach according to criteria related to health-promoting architecture, including spatial orientation, accessibility, environmental safety, sensory comfort, social interaction, and reduction of stress and behavioral symptoms. RESULTS: The analysis showed that clear functional layouts, spatial zoning, and intuitive wayfinding reduce disorientation and improve patient independence. Important elements include appropriate colors, visual identification features, natural lighting, contact with nature, and ergonomic and safe equipment. Communal spaces support social interaction, reduce isolation, and enhance therapeutic processes. These solutions may reduce stress, aggressive behaviors, and improve quality of care. CONCLUSIONS: Designing geriatric psychiatric wards according to the needs of people with dementia supports treatment effectiveness and user safety. Integration of architectural knowledge with psychiatry and environmental psychology enables the creation of health-promoting environments. The findings may support modernization of existing wards and the design of new facilities, while indicating the need for further research on the impact of therapeutic environments on clinical outcomes and patient well-being in long-term psychiatric care settings for older adults.
