items.title: Detecting AI-Induced Risk Blind Spots in Technical Program Management Through Human–AI Decision Comparison
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support technical program managers in identifying delivery risks, but improved productivity does not necessarily imply more complete risk recognition. A critical failure mode arises when a manager initially identifies a material risk and later removes it after encountering an AI-generated assessment. This paper develops a human–AI decision-comparison method for detecting such omissions without equating disagreement with error. The framework records an unaided initial risk register, randomly assigns decision makers to a human-only second pass, ordinary AI assistance, or AI assistance with a structured challenge step, and assesses final decisions against independently adjudicated scenario risks. It distinguishes risk discovery, risk retention, and severity-weighted coverage using explicit transition measures and a multilevel comparison strategy. items.title: Differentiating Agricultural Tractor Brands and Models through User-Reported Quality Profiles
items.abstract: User experience with agricultural tractors is multidimensional and can be obscured by a single brand-level score. This study analysed 140 tractor-evaluation questionnaires covering 21 tractor brands and 44 detailed quality attributes rated on a seven-point scale. Descriptive analyses used the complete sample, whereas formal brand differentiation was restricted to six brands represented by at least five questionnaires (N = 108). Attribute-wise differences were evaluated by the Kruskal–Wallis test, epsilon-squared effect sizes, Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction, and stratified bootstrap confidence intervals. To test whether the 44-attribute profiles contained reproducible brand information beyond univariate contrasts, a shrinkage linear discriminant model was evaluated by stratified five-fold cross-validation and a label-permutation test. Spare-parts availability (6.26), engine reliability (6.16), and forward visibility (6.14) were the highest-rated attributes, whereas storage availability (4.64), passenger space (4.89), and vibration damping (4.94) were lowest. The strongest brand differentiation occurred for ease of radiator cleaning (ε² = 0.508), vibration damping (0.499), overall comfort (0.460), rear hydraulic-coupler access (0.448), and cab lighting (0.440). Cross-validated balanced brand-classification accuracy reached 0.371, compared with a six-class chance level of 0.167 (permutation p = 0.002). At model level, within-brand centering separated model-specific domain profiles from the corresponding brand baseline; 12 models represented by at least three users were visualized. The results show that practical tractor quality is structured by specific ergonomic, maintainability, reliability, and ownership attributes and that these detailed profiles contain reproducible information at both brand and model levels.

items.title: Digital media as pedagogy: A human-centred decision approach for higher education digital media integration
items.abstract: This poster positions digital media (DM) assets as pedagogical decisions, arguing that their value lies not in technical sophistication, but in how effectively a medium supports learning within a given educational context (Mayer, 2020). Aligned with the ASCILITE 2026 subtheme of Human Centred Learning Design, this work introduces Digital Media as Pedagogy (DMaP), a decision-making approach that supports intentional DM selection in higher education. DMaP foregrounds pedagogical relationships and learner needs over technology guided choice, demonstrating that the suitability of different media forms varies depending on learning outcomes and the specific educational context. Meaningful media decision making requires strong collaboration between Learning Experience Designers (LEDs) and DM teams. Media design is frequently treated as a production task, downstream of the core learning content design (Thompson & Harris, 2025). This limits pedagogically aligned innovation positioning media specialists as technical implementers rather than pedagogical collaborators. Research on educational video and DM highlights that design decisions such as pacing, length, and interactivity, have a greater impact on engagement and learning than technical, even aesthetic, sophistication (Guo et al., 2014). This poster reframes the LED/DM relationship as a critical collaborative practice where expertise in pedagogy, accessibility, analytics and media production intersect. Early and ongoing collaboration supports more intentional and sustainable media design. This approach has informed changes to practice, including earlier involvement of DM specialists in subject development meetings. Positioning DM teams within early pedagogical discussions enables more cohesive alignment between learning intent and media, moving away from a more transactional style of interaction between LEDs and DM team members. The DMaP approach integrates five interconnected design lenses. The lens of pedagogical intent draws on Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) to examine whether a medium is pedagogically appropriate for specific content and learner contexts, while also legitimising collaboration across pedagogical, technological, and content expertise (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). The Cognitive Engagement lens applies the ICAP framework to examine observable learner activity, recognising that passive, active, constructive, and interactive modes each have contextual pedagogical value rather than forming a simple hierarchy (Chi & Wylie, 2014). Accessibility and Inclusion are foregrounded through Universal Design for Learning (UDL), positioning flexibility and learner choice as pedagogical strengths. This is realised through multiple means of engagement, representation and action and expressions (CAST 2024). Evidence-based Tool Selection draws on research demonstrating that digital media effectiveness varies significantly by context and design rather than novelty and considers pedagogical soundness and institutional viability (Kirkwood & Price, 2014). The final lens examines Integration and Learning Systems, recognising that, from our experience, media effectiveness appears to be influenced by LMS integration and breaks from cognitive load. DMaP questions the conventional matching of digital tool to task which tends to favour novelty over pedagogical fit. Instead, it proposes a human centred decision logic where media is selected because it aligns with intended cognitive engagement. A pedagogical approach to digital media enables accessible participation and remains feasible within institutional constraints. DMaP offers an appliable, theoretically informed approach for learning designers and DM teams.

items.title: Digitalidades deconstructivas: La inteligencia artificial generativa como pharmakon en la Educación Rural Colombiana
items.abstract: La irrupción de la inteligencia artificial generativa en la escuela suele leerse desde dos posiciones simétricas: la adopción instrumental y la prohibición defensiva. El objetivo de este artículo es proponer un marco teórico-metodológico que supere ese dilema desde una institución educativa rural de baja conectividad en Cajibío, Cauca (Colombia). Se trata de un artículo de reflexión derivado de una tesis doctoral en curso, elaborado mediante análisis hermenéutico-conceptual de fuentes de la deconstrucción, la teoría de sistemas sociales, la crítica de la digitalidad y las epistemologías del Sur, contrastadas con antecedentes empíricos recientes sobre inteligencia artificial generativa, educación y ruralidad y traducidas en un diseño de investigación basada en diseño. Como resultado se construyen tres conceptos articulados: la superficialidad cognitiva, entendida como procesamiento del saber sin reingreso; la deconstrucción digital, operación breve y situada que irrita esa superficialidad a través de la interfaz algorítmica; y las digitalidades deconstructivas, estado plural en el que la reducción de la superficialidad se vuelve expectativa del sistema escolar. Se propone, además, la noción de acoplamiento pharmaco-deconstructivo, según la cual la decisión pedagógica no versa sobre adoptar o prohibir, sino sobre regular la dosis de irritación, y un diseño de contraste con tres condiciones, reporte estratificado y criterios de refutación declarados de antemano. Se concluye que la escasez de conectividad, leída como lugar de enunciación y no como déficit, exige pensar la mediación docente asincrónica como condición de una justicia cognitiva situada.

items.title: Discovering Agentic AI: Discovery, Preservation, and Proof in AI and Agentic Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems evolve beyond conversational interfaces into multi-step workflows capable of retrieving information, maintaining state, invoking tools, delegating tasks, and acting across external systems, electronic discovery faces increasingly complex evidentiary questions. A user-facing transcript or current system configuration may not establish what information an AI system received, what instructions and controls governed its behavior, what actions it was authorized to perform, or what consequences resulted from a disputed historical execution.This white paper examines the application of United States federal civil discovery and evidence law to AI and agentic systems. Drawing on emerging judicial decisions and established electronic discovery principles, it analyzes relevance, proportionality, preservation, possession, custody or control, privilege, production, authentication, and expert proof. It identifies potential evidentiary sources across system and developer instructions, model configurations, retrieval-augmented generation, tool and API schemas, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, agent memory, orchestration, delegated authority, execution traces, configuration histories, and downstream business records.The paper advances reconstructable execution state as a proposition-centered analytical framework for identifying the minimum historically accurate evidence necessary to evaluate a disputed AI execution. It distinguishes technical capability from authorization, attempted actions from completed effects, present-day configurations from historical conditions, and contemporaneous records from inference or later reconstruction.Integrating recent AI-related discovery developments with practical preservation, collection, and evidentiary methods, the paper proposes an execution-centered approach to identifying relevant sources, reconstructing historical system behavior, and evaluating evidentiary reliability. Its central argument is that agentic AI does not require a separate discovery regime, but rather a more rigorous application of existing law to dynamic, distributed, and version-dependent evidence.

items.title: Discovering High Level Patterns from Simulation Traces
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are unable to reliably reason about specific physical systems. Attempts to imbue LLMs with knowledge of the necessary physics concepts have shown great promise, but explainability and validation remain open challenges. An emerging alternative is tooling, where LLMs can query physical simulators and use the resulting simulation traces as context for validation. This approach suffers from poor scalability since simulation traces contain large volumes of fine-grained numerical and semantic data. We show that translating simulation traces to a sparse representation of ‘high-level’ structural patterns leads to more effective interpretation by LLMs. We propose an unsupervised learning scheme to perform this translation, or annotation, via program synthesis. Our learning results in a library of programs that act as pattern detectors which can translate simulation logs to sparse, annotated pattern sequences. The detected patterns may optionally be guided by human experts via string labels (rigid collision, stretching spring, etc.). We show, using a recent physics benchmark, that such annotated representations are more amenable to natural language reasoning about specific physical systems. The synthesised programs serve as transparent, explainable functions that map system states to a sparse and efficient annotation space. As an example application, we show how goals within physical systems that are specified in natural language may be converted to reward programs which are maximised to find solutions.

items.title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

items.title: Do LLMs Understand Network Traces? A Comparative Study of Reasoning over Raw and Filtered Traffic Data
items.abstract: The effective delivery and monitoring of ICT services rely heavily on network traffic analysis. However, interpreting complex packet captures remains a challenging task that requires substantial technical expertise. Large language models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate network traffic in- vestigation, yet their reliability in packet-level field extraction and flow-level sequence reconstruction remains an open research question. This study proposes a reproducible, question-answering- based evaluation methodology to assess the capabilities of LLMs in network trace analysis. Using real-world benign traffic from the CICIDS2017 dataset, we evaluate multiple models against a human-generated ground truth, comparing their performance on raw textual traffic dumps and protocol-filtered representations. Model responses are assessed through an automated LLM- as-a-judge pipeline, validated against human evaluations. The results demonstrate that protocol filtering significantly reduces prompt overhead while improving answer accuracy by reducing incorrect responses. These findings highlight the importance of protocol-aware traffic filtering as an effective optimization for improving the efficiency and reliability of LLM-assisted network management.

items.title: Does explanation correctness matter? Linking computational XAI evaluation to human understanding
items.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods are commonly evaluated using functional correctness metrics, also called faithfulness or fidelity, which estimate how closely an explanation reflects the model’s reasoning. Higher correctness is assumed to produce better human understanding, but this link has not been tested with controlled levels. We conducted a user study ( N = 200 ) that manipulated explanation correctness at four levels (100%, 85%, 70%, 55%) in a synthetic time series classification task where participants could not rely on domain knowledge or visual intuition. Explanations were constructed to resemble feature attributions, with correctness defined against a known ground truth rather than estimated from a trained model. Participants predicted a simulated AI’s decisions from these explanations (forward simulation), and we used their forward simulation accuracy as a proxy for understanding. Correctness affected forward simulation accuracy, but not at every level: accuracy dropped at 70% and 55% relative to 100%, with no further reduction below 70% and no conclusive difference between 85% and 100%. Lower correctness reduced how many participants predicted accurately rather than lowering accuracy uniformly, and even with fully correct explanations, only a subset of participants predicted well above chance. In exploratory analyses, some participants predicted decisions accurately but described the wrong pattern when asked what the AI used, and self-reported ratings correlated with forward simulation accuracy only when explanations were fully correct. These findings suggest that, for feature-attribution-style explanations, not all differences in functional correctness translate to differences in human understanding, highlighting the need to validate functional metrics against human outcomes.

items.title: Dressed in Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking of MLLMs via Visual Trust Bias
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing, yet their safety remains a critical concern, especially under jailbreak attempts. Existing MLLM jailbreaks either inject fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesize toxic visual cues to achieve text-driven attack intents. In contrast, a more practical MLLM jailbreak emphasizes enhancing attack efficacy directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs. We address this problem by proposing Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a new jailbreak framework that exploits a previously overlooked attack surface: MLLMs exhibit an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, which enables transferable and stealthy jailbreaks. VTBA constructs a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input pair to the most relevant one, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, thereby leveraging credible visual cues to override safety refusals while preserving naturalness. We further construct a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs to evaluate jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong MLLMs, revealing a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. items.title: EAL/D students’ constructions of agency in AI technology-assisted learning environments: A case from the field of media and communication studies
items.abstract: The use of generative AI (GenAI) technologies has become increasingly prevalent across Australian higher education. As these tools become an integral part of learning, they also raise concerns about over-reliance and learner agency (Resnick, 2024), authorship, ownership, and problematic forms of co-creation (Bozkurt, 2024). In Australia, 31% of the student population identify as having English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) (Australian Government Department of Education, 2024). Apart from cultural and linguistic challenges, EAL/D students also need to adapt to new academic expectations and practices that account for the impacts of GenAI technologies (Kebble, 2023). Given the unique challenges facing EAL/D student cohorts with their diverse pre-existing technological backgrounds, a gap exists in understanding how EAL/D students perceive their own work and academic contributions in relation to their use of GenAI tools. This study explores EAL/D students’ AI-assisted learning experiences and perspectives on agency through qualitative interviews conducted with 34 Master of Digital Communication students over 18 months. Findings suggest that EAL/D students are instinctively adjusting and adapting their learning practices as they engage with these technologies and making agentic decisions that support their learning. To maintain what they considered to be original and creative in their work, students developed several strategies to distinguish their own work from AI-generated output. We also found that as EAL/D students’ engagement with AI increases, they develop critical self-scrutiny. They maintain agency and ownership over their assessed work by ensuring that their (human) creativity remains central throughout the learning process. While there are some commonalities, the students in our study took diverse paths, with some students developing more nuanced and balanced approaches to using AI than others. For these students, the shift enabled them to integrate GenAI strategically while maintaining their own voice and sense of agency.

items.title: EEG Theta Power as an Indicator of Cognitive Workload in Student Pilots
items.abstract: Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4–8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. NASA-TLX results similarly indicated increased mental demand, effort, and frustration in the scenario associated with the highest cognitive workload. However, correlation analysis revealed a weak and inconsistent relationship between subjective workload ratings and EEG-derived theta measures across participants, with no clear or statistically significant overall association at the group level. These preliminary results indicate that scalp-recorded theta activity is sensitive to changes in task difficulty during flight simulation. However, given the exploratory nature of the study, the absence of flight-performance metrics, and the lack of strong correlation with subjective ratings, theta-band modulation should be interpreted as an index of task demand rather than a fully consolidated operational workload estimator.

items.title: Effect of Guided ChatGPT Use on Documented Clinical Reasoning and Its Retention Among Emergency Medicine Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background: Clinical reasoning is a core competency in emergency medicine, and its structured teaching remains challenging. Generative artificial intelligence (ChatGPT) may represent a useful educational tool, but its impact on learning consolidation beyond immediate benefit remains uncertain. We assessed whether guided use of ChatGPT improves immediate documented clinical reasoning performance without compromising its retention over time. Methods: A single-center, two-arm, parallel-group, exploratory randomized controlled trial was conducted in the emergency department of Mohammed VI University Hospital, Marrakech, Morocco. Sixty medical students (5th–6th year) were randomized 1:1, using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes generated by an independent investigator, to a ChatGPT group (simulated clinical cases with guided GPT-4o assistance) or a control group (no assistance); outcome assessors were blinded to group and time point, although participants could not be blinded to the intervention received. The primary outcome was the total Revised-IDEA (R-IDEA) score (/10), measured immediately after the intervention (T0) and again one month later under unassisted conditions (T1), analyzed by analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusted for the T0 score. Results: All 60 participants were followed at T0 and T1, with no loss to follow-up. At T0, the R-IDEA score was significantly higher in the ChatGPT group (median 9.50 vs 8.50; p < 0.001; r = 0.96). At T1, the pattern reversed: the ChatGPT group showed a significant decline (median Δ = −0.75), whereas the control group improved (Δ = +1.00; p < 0.001; r = 0.96). ANCOVA confirmed a group effect at T1 favoring the control group (adjusted difference = 0.48 points, 95% CI 0.16–0.80; p = 0.004; partial η² = 0.136). Perceived confidence and benefit in the ChatGPT group were not correlated with actual performance change. Conclusions: Conclusions: Guided ChatGPT assistance improves immediate documented clinical reasoning performance, but this benefit does not persist at one month and is accompanied by poorly calibrated learner confidence. These findings support structured pedagogical oversight of generative AI in medical education, combined with active learning-consolidation strategies to ensure durable skill acquisition. Trial registration: ISRCTN registry ISRCTN13261015, registered 3 August 2026. Retrospectively registered.

items.title: Effect of Working Environment on Employee Performance in the Hospitality Industry in Rwanda: A Case of Lemigo Hotel
items.abstract: This study examined the effect of the working environment on employee performance in the hospitality industry in Rwanda, using Lemigo Hotel as a case study.Specifically, it assessed the effect of physical ergonomics and safety, open communication, professional growth and development, and work-life balance on employee performance.A mixed-methods descriptive research design was adopted, combining quantitative and qualitative approaches.Data were collected from a census of 198 employees using structured questionnaires, interview guides, and documentary review, and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression in SPSS, while qualitative data were analysed thematically.The findings revealed a strong positive relationship between the combined working-environment factors and employee performance (R = 0.799), with the four predictors jointly explaining 67.4% of the variance (R² = 0.674; adjusted R² = 0.641).The regression coefficients showed that physical ergonomics and safety (B = 0.353, p = 0.025), open communication (B = 0.472, p = 0.003), professional growth and development (B = 0.676, p = 0.001), and work-life balance (B = 0.353, p = 0.009) each had a significant positive effect on employee performance, with no multicollinearity (VIF = 1.246-2.491).All four null hypotheses were rejected.The study concludes that a safe, communicative, developmental, and balanced working environment is a fundamental determinant of employee performance in the hospitality industry.It recommends that Lemigo Hotel invest in ergonomic and safety upgrades, institutionalize transparent communication channels, expand career-development pathways, and strengthen work-life balance policies to sustain and improve employee performance.

items.title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.

items.title: Emotional Work between “Reasonable Words” and “My Words”: Practices and Boundaries of Generative AI in Romantic Relationships
items.abstract: Drawing on emotion work theory and an AI-mediated communication perspective, this study uses thematic analysis to examine how emotion work is reorganized when generative AI becomes involved as a third party in communication between romantic partners. The findings indicate that some interviewees associate AI support with less concern about being judged and a lower burden of interpersonal reciprocity. They draw on its explanations and suggestions to make sense of emotions, formulate messages, and plan communication. At the same time, users need to screen and modify the generated content, and check whether the emotional attitude in it is in line with their own feelings, so as to form “authenticity work”. After the generated content is adopted, responding to the partner, fulfilling the repair arrangement, and making continuous adjustments according to the interaction between the two parties still require the input of the parties, reflecting the “limited entrustment” of emotional work. Research shows that generative AI changes the completion process of emotional work by sharing some tasks and bringing new expression management and provides an empirical basis for understanding technology-aided sincerity and relationship input.

items.title: Employment Prospect Perceptions and Learning Agency Among Chinese Undergraduate Art and Design Students
items.abstract: Background As the art and design industry faces overall pressure and employment adjustments in China, how students' employment evaluations relate to their current learning behaviors requires further investigation. Grounded in Social Cognitive Career Theory, this study examined the associations among employment prospect perceptions, career self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and learning agency. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from April to July 2026 with 591 undergraduate art and design students from four application-oriented universities in China. A two-stage partial least squares structural equation model was employed, modeling employment prospect perceptions as a formative higher-order construct comprising absolute and comparative evaluation components, while estimating its direct association with learning agency and indirect associations via career self-efficacy and outcome expectations. Bootstrap resampling was used for inference, and exploratory comparisons across academic majors were conducted using permutation tests with Bonferroni correction. Results Career self-efficacy was positively associated with learning agency (β = .598, 95% CI [.488, .696]), and the specific indirect association from employment prospect perceptions to learning agency via career self-efficacy was .263 (95% CI [.205, .323]). The direct association between employment prospect perceptions and learning agency (β = .053, p = .239) and the association between outcome expectations and learning agency (β = .100, p = .101) did not reach significance. The model explained 48.0% of the variance in learning agency. After correction, none of the 18 between-major path comparisons reached significance. Conclusions Career self-efficacy serves as an important linking factor connecting employment prospect perceptions with learning agency. The study provides evidence for applying SCCT in career preparatory learning contexts and suggests that career support may integrate employment information with professional competence experiences. The temporal order and causal direction of these associations require longitudinal research for validation.

items.title: Empowerment, delegation and vision awareness: motivational pathways to workplace creativity
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how employee empowerment and task delegation influence workplace creativity through harmonious and obsessive work passion, and whether organizational vision awareness (OVA) strengthens these motivational pathways in a public sector context. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 533 employees across two Namibian public sector ministries using stratified random sampling. Employee self-reports were matched with supervisor ratings of incremental and radical creativity to reduce common method bias. Structural equation modeling tested indirect and conditional relationships among empowerment, delegation, work passion and creativity. Findings Empowerment and task delegation are indirectly related to creativity through distinct forms of work passion. Harmonious passion predicts both incremental and radical creativity, whereas obsessive passion is primarily linked to incremental creativity. OVA strengthens selected motivational pathways, showing that shared vision enhances the effectiveness of leadership practices in fostering creativity. Originality/value This study demonstrates that empowerment and delegation operate through differentiated passion-based mechanisms rather than uniform effects. By distinguishing between incremental and radical creativity, it clarifies how motivational processes translate managerial practices into distinct creative outcomes. It further extends the literature by identifying OVA as a boundary condition and by providing evidence from an underexplored African public sector context.

items.title: Enabling AI-ready medical graduates: A working group approach to curriculum and assessment change in a graduate medical program
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming clinical practice, and digital-health and assessment frameworks increasingly identify capabilities that involve using AI. Translating these expectations into a crowded, vertically integrated medical curriculum is a substantial implementation challenge. This case study describes how one Australian graduate medical program has approached integrating AI literacy education, teaching with AI and assessment reform. A cross-functional working group, convened by the Dean of Medicine and chaired by the first author, comprising academic, clinical, professional, library and student members and reporting to the School Executive, has coordinated the program’s early response through monthly meetings, program planning day sessions and engagement with grassroots pilots, including a trial of an AI-powered communication skills simulation platform. We describe the challenges encountered: defining AI literacy content without a settled national curriculum, negotiating curriculum space across all year levels, sustaining communication among diverse stakeholders, developing staff capability across attitudes ranging from enthusiasm to sustained concern, responding to student concerns about AI-enabled learning tools, and redesigning assessment to comply with institution-wide reform while preserving a programmatic assessment system. We share practical lessons for other programs, arguing that an enabling, relationship-centred approach may help coordinate change.

items.abstract: This study examined how Biology teachers engage students through Project-Based Learning (PBL) in six-day lower secondary schools in Gasabo District, Rwanda, guided by three objectives: teachers' understanding of PBL, their design and implementation of PBL activities, and PBL's contribution to students' motivation.A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was adopted within the pragmatic paradigm, with all 30 Biology teachers in the six schools included through census sampling.Data were collected using a questionnaire, a semi-structured interview guide, and a classroom observation checklist, and triangulated across the three sources; quantitative data were analyzed in SPSS Version 26 using descriptive statistics and multiple regression, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically.Teachers showed a strong theoretical understanding of PBL (M = 4.00-4.13)but a comparatively weaker command of implementation and assessment procedures (M = 3.70-3.73),a gap attributed to limited time, large classes, and insufficient materials rather than to any deficit in conceptual knowledge.Effective PBL activities were curriculum-aligned, collaborative, inquiry-based, and teacher-facilitated.Authentic, real-life projects emerged as the strongest predictor of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, with the largest effect on cognitive engagement (β = 0.451, p = .001).PBL is an effective, learner-centred approach for engaging Biology students, and its full potential is currently constrained more by institutional and resource conditions than by teachers' understanding of, or commitment to, the approach.Strengthening teacher capacity in PBL implementation and assessment, and providing adequate instructional time and materials, is recommended.

items.title: ENGAJAMENTO COGNITIVO EM ESCOLARES DA REDE PÚBLICA E SUA ASSOCIAÇÃO COM INDICADORES ANTROPOMÉTRICOS
items.abstract: O engajamento cognitivo representa o investimento do estudante no processo de aprendizagem, envolvendo atenção, participação, organização, persistência e conclusão de atividades escolares. Embora o estado nutricional seja considerado um possível fator relacionado ao desenvolvimento infantil, sua associação com indicadores de engajamento e resultados escolares permanece inconsistente. O presente estudo teve como objetivo avaliar o engajamento cognitivo de escolares da rede pública municipal de Vassouras-RJ e investigar sua associação com o escore-Z de índice de massa corporal para idade. Trata-se de estudo observacional, transversal, quantitativo, descritivo e analítico, realizado com 178 escolares provenientes de três escolas públicas. O índice de massa corporal foi convertido em escore-Z para idade segundo a referência da Organização Mundial da Saúde. O engajamento cognitivo foi avaliado inicialmente por oito itens ordinais de autorrelato. A estrutura dimensional foi examinada por análise fatorial exploratória baseada em matriz de correlação policórica, com avaliação pelo índice de Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin, teste de esfericidade de Bartlett, análise paralela e confiabilidade pelo ômega de McDonald. O escore final foi composto por seis itens. A associação principal foi avaliada pela correlação de Spearman, com intervalo de confiança de 95% obtido por 5.000 reamostragens bootstrap, e por modelo linear ajustado por idade, sexo e escola. Entre os 167 escolares com dados antropométricos completos, 63,5% apresentaram eutrofia, 34,1% excesso de peso e 2,4% magreza. Os itens apresentaram adequação satisfatória à análise fatorial (KMO=0,80; teste de Bartlett, p<0,001), estrutura unidimensional e confiabilidade satisfatória após a exclusão de dois itens (ω=0,83). Não foi observada associação estatisticamente significativa entre o escore-Z de IMC e o engajamento cognitivo (n=161; ρ de Spearman=-0,10; IC95%: -0,25 a +0,05; p=0,21). O modelo ajustado corroborou esse resultado. Os achados indicam que o escore-Z de IMC, isoladamente, não explicou a variabilidade do engajamento cognitivo na população estudada, reforçando o caráter multifatorial do envolvimento escolar.

items.title: Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT): A human-centred assessment framework for the Generative AI era
items.abstract: Generative AI is changing how students complete assessments and demonstrate what they know. As AI tools become part of everyday study, final assessment submissions alone may not provide sufficient evidence of how students think, solve problems, or develop understanding throughout the learning process. This paper introduces Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT), a human-centred assessment framework designed for the AI era. Rather than focusing on whether students use AI, EVT focuses on designing assessments that generate multiple forms of evidence to support judgements about student learning. The framework is built around three connected elements: visible thinking, process evidence, and capability validation. The paper draws on the design of a new Applied IT degree and includes a detailed example from the first-year Networking Fundamentals course to illustrate the application of the EVT framework in practice. The paper argues that the real challenge is not detecting AI use but designing assessments that provide evidence to support judgements about students’ learning and capability. By extending assessment beyond final products to include evidence of thinking, process and demonstrated competence, EVT offers a practical approach to assessment design that keeps people, not technology, at the centre of learning.

items.title: Enhancing cultural sensitivity in university artificial intelligence principles
items.abstract: Universities’ education-related artificial intelligence (AI) principles are vital statements that accessibly outline the institutions’ stances towards the technology’s use in learning. Ensuring the cultural sensitivity of these principles is vital given today’s superdiversity in higher education. This paper presents insights from research examining the cultural sensitivity of these principles, using Australian universities as its case study. The research covers 42 Australian universities, with AI principle content from 28 universities analysed using a qualitative content analysis. The findings show that the idea of cultural sensitivity is generally addressed at a surface level. The paper argues that all universities not only need to provide robust, publicly accessible educational AI principles, but also actively integrate cultural sensitivity into these principles. Based on the paper’s research insights, a novel framework is provided to support this integration.

items.title: ERGONOMIA EM EVENTOS: IMPORTÂNCIA E CONTRIBUIÇÕES PARA A FORMAÇÃO PROFISSIONAL DOS ESTUDANTES DO CURSO SUPERIOR DE TECNOLOGIA EM EVENTOS DA FATEC JUNDIAÍ
items.abstract: A ergonomia constitui um campo de conhecimento importante para a promoção da saúde, segurança, conforto e eficiência nas atividades profissionais, com aplicação no setor de eventos. Este estudo teve como objetivo analisar a importância da ergonomia e suas contribuições para a formação acadêmica e profissional dos estudantes do Curso Superior de Tecnologia em Eventos da Fatec Jundiaí. A pesquisa caracterizou-se como aplicada, de abordagem quali-quantitativa e caráter exploratório e descritivo, desenvolvida por meio de pesquisa bibliográfica e de campo. A coleta de dados ocorreu entre junho e setembro de 2026, mediante aplicação de questionário eletrônico composto por nove questões objetivas e uma dissertativa. Participaram 19 estudantes, dos quais dez responderam à questão aberta, constituindo o corpus da análise qualitativa. Os dados quantitativos foram analisados por meio de estatística descritiva, enquanto as dez respostas dissertativas foram examinadas por análise temática descritiva e interpretativa, organizadas em cinco categorias. Os resultados demonstraram que 94,7% dos participantes concordaram totalmente com a necessidade de considerar aspectos ergonômicos no planejamento de eventos, enquanto 57,9% reconheceram sua importância em todas as etapas de realização. Quanto ao preparo para identificar situações ergonômicas, 63,2% manifestaram concordância total. A análise qualitativa evidenciou percepções relacionadas à segurança, ao conforto, à acessibilidade, à organização dos espaços e à qualidade dos eventos. Concluiu-se que a ergonomia representa um conhecimento relevante para a formação do Tecnólogo em eventos, destacando-se a necessidade de fortalecer a articulação entre os fundamentos teóricos e sua aplicação prática no contexto profissional.

items.title: Ergonomic Risk Factors and Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders among Rice Harvesting Workers of Jorhat, Assam, India
items.abstract: Manual rice harvesting in India involves long hours of repetitive work, awkward postures, and workers have little ergonomic training. This study identified the ergonomic risk factors and work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) among rice harvesting workers. A cross-sectional survey of 100 workers was conducted in two villages of Titabor block, Jorhat district, Assam. Data were collected using an interview schedule, observation and still photography. Postures were scored with the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA). Perceived joint discomfort, perceived exertion (RPE) and WMSD severity and frequency were rated on scales, and associations were tested using correlation analysis and a t-test. Respondents were mostly women (68%) aged 31–40 years (48%). Workers worked 7–8 hours a day, mainly standing with a forward bend. RULA scores ranged from 5 to 7 (medium to high risk), with the highest scores for harvesting and threshing (7). Perceived exertion was highest for harvesting (4.20) and threshing (4.09). Discomfort was greatest at the waist (3.58), shoulder (3.54) and neck (3.51). Low back pain (88%), shoulder pain (86%) and neck pain (84%) were most common; 35% of workers felt pain always, and 28% reported acute pain. Age, years of involvement and perceived joint discomfort correlated significantly with work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) frequency and severity (p < 0.05).

items.title: Ethical Governance of AI in Public Sector Human Resource Management: Challenges of Indonesia's Digital Bureaucracy
items.abstract: The deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) has reshaped recruitment, performance evaluation, talent mapping, and workforce planning across both private and public sectors. While AI-based systems are widely associated with efficiency, objectivity, and data-driven decision-making, their use in public institutions also raises ethical problems concerning transparency, accountability, fairness, and algorithmic bias. AI systems trained on historical data can reproduce discrimination and reinforce structural inequalities. This article examines ethical AI governance in public HRM by exploring the interaction between human–AI collaboration, algorithmic bias, and institutional accountability. Using a qualitativeconceptual approach grounded in a critical literature review of 41 sources published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by analysis of recent Indonesian regulatory and institutional documents (UU No. 20/2023 on ASN, BKN Circular Letter No. 9/2025, the ASN Digital platform, and the GARUDA AI program), the study finds that Indonesia’s digital bureaucracy faces four structural challenges: a governance gap between AI adoption and regulatory readiness; limited institutional capacity for algorithmic oversight; insufficient AI literacy among HR officials; and the absence of a standardized algorithmic-ethics audit. The article contributes a four-layer ethical-governance model regulatory, institutional, technical, and capability calibrated to Indonesia’s publicadministration context, and argues that AI in public HRM must remain anchored in democratic values, social justice, and human-centred oversight.

items.title: Evaluating Generative AI in Chemistry Prelabs: Efficiency Gains without Measurable Learning Benefits
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has raised questions regarding their impact on students’ information literacy (IL) and cognitive processes. In this study, we investigated how generative AI influences undergraduate students’ performance and perceptions in an inorganic chemistry prelaboratory assignment consisting in gathering and elaborating information relevant to the experiments. Second-year chemistry students completed two prelab tasks: one with generative AI support and one without AI. Students reported that generative AI support significantly reduced time dedicated to prelab elaboration. They also perceived AI-assisted tasks as easier and faster, rated AI-generated information as less clear and precise than traditional sources, and frequently expressed concerns about its reliability. However, no statistically significant differences were observed in instructor-evaluated scores between AI-supported and non-AI prelabs. These results indicate that students predominantly valued AI for efficiency. Interpreted through a Cognitive Load Theory lens, the reduction in time and search effort is consistent with a possible decrease in task-related logistical demands.

items.title: Evaluating Interpretation Risks in Interactive What-If Scenarios and Mitigating with HypotheX
items.abstract: Human-centered XAI conceptualizes explanations as external representations of model behavior intended to support users’ reasoning and sensemaking, rather than as self-contained artifacts that directly convey understanding. Because their interpretation is shaped by users’ cognitive processes and contextual circumstances, understanding emerges through active engagement in formulating, testing, and refining hypotheses. In exploratory settings, where relevant questions and factors are not fully specified in advance, such engagement relies on iterative questioning, experimentation, and revision, typically mediated through interactive visualization. Hypothetical Scenario (HS)–based XAI methods operationalize this exploratory mode of explanation by enabling users to manipulate input conditions and observe resulting changes in model outputs. Through what-if testing, HS externalizes users’ reasoning processes by instantiating hypotheses as concrete interactions whose consequences become observable. Exploratory interaction, however, is not cognitively neutral. Prior work in cognitive science and human–computer interaction shows that reasoning during exploration is systematically shaped by cognitive biases such as anchoring, availability, and salience. In HS-based exploration, these biases can influence scenario selection, input sampling, outcome comparison, and the sequencing of interactions, leading to incomplete or misleading interpretations even when explanations are technically faithful. Such biases do not manifest as incorrect explanations, but as characteristic interaction behaviors that signal elevated risks of misinterpretation. Accordingly, this paper examines bias-related interpretation risks in HS-based XAI and evaluates whether targeted interface design safeguards can reduce bias-prone interaction patterns. We introduce HypotheX, an interactive HS-based XAI system, and show that interface-level interventions can mitigate some—though not all—such risks.

items.title: Evaluation-Verification Reward for Consistent Multi-Reference Image Editing
items.abstract: While recent image editing models have made rapid progress, multi-reference editing remains challenging, particularly in maintaining visual consistency across references and ensuring overall visual harmony. Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for text-to-image generation and single-image editing, but its extension to multi-reference editing is hindered by the absence of suitable reward models that capture multi-image relational constraints. Moreover, naively using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as zero-shot evaluators faces a key tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and the limited deductive power of short-form judgments. We address these issues with a Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward (EVR). EVR decomposes evaluation into distinct visual criteria; for each criterion, an MLLM Evaluator generates multiple candidate hypotheses, and a Verifier checks each claim against visible evidence before reward aggregation, producing more reliable and fine-grained reward signals. Together with a scalable data pipeline, our method enables RL fine-tuning of off-the-shelf editors without architectural changes. Extensive experiments show substantial gains over the base Qwen-Image-Edit, improving consistency and harmony while remaining competitive with strong closed-source editors such as NanoBanana. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/EVR.

items.title: EviDARL: Evidence-Centric Dual-Agent Reasoning via Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Table Question Answering
items.abstract: Despite advances in LLM-based table reasoning, most studies focus on single-table settings. Multi-table QA requires multi-hop reasoning over complex table relationships and evidence dispersed across long contexts, often without verifiable intermediate traces. To address these challenges, we introduce EviDA, an evidence-centric dual-agent framework comprising an Evidence Construction Agent and a Reasoning and Answering Agent. The Evidence Construction Agent generates and executes table-manipulation programs over complete tables to produce question-specific evidence and verifiable intermediate traces, simplifying subsequent reasoning. The Reasoning and Answering Agent then performs multi-hop reasoning over this evidence to derive final answers. We further introduce EviDARL, which combines agent-specific fine-grained rewards with parameter-efficient alternating reinforcement learning to improve collaboration between the agents. By optimizing each agent in turn while holding the other fixed, EviDARL enables bidirectional adaptation between evidence construction and answer reasoning. Experiments on MMQA and TQA-Bench demonstrate that EviDARL substantially outperforms competitive open-model and multi-table reasoning baselines under constrained model and training budgets.

items.title: EvoCoT: Co-evolving generation and verification for LLM-based optimization autoformulation
items.abstract: Formulating optimization models from natural-language specifications is a major bottleneck in engineering decision-making, requiring both domain expertise and strict modeling discipline. Existing large language model (LLM) approaches often produce formulations that are executable yet semantically incorrect, or structurally invalid under solver constraints. Evolutionary Chain-of-Thought Optimization (EvoCoT) is introduced as a co-evolutionary autoformulation framework that treats model synthesis as guided discrete search over reasoning–code pairs rather than one-shot generation. EvoCoT couples three mechanisms in a single feedback loop: reasoning-first evolutionary search over a population of decoded programs, memory-guided exemplar retrieval, and a co-evolving verifier that provides structural-faithfulness feedback beyond static solver checks. Experiments on eight benchmark suites show consistent improvements over strong zero-shot baselines and competitive performance against agentic and fine-tuned systems, with the largest gains on difficult industrial-scale tasks. Attribution analyses under matched search budgets show that the population-level evolutionary search at the core of the framework accounts for these accuracy gains. The verifier and memory complement this search with reliability and triage rather than additional accuracy: a graded, execution-grounded trust signal for ranking surviving formulations, and an auditable, leakage-controlled library of validated formulations.

items.title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
items.abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.

items.title: Explainability Metrics for Object Detection Models
items.abstract: Object detection models based on deep learning achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in many applications, but their predictions are difficult to interpret. Existing explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques for computer vision mostly focus on image classification, and their direct extension to object detection is non-trivial, as detectors must explain both what was detected (class) and where it was detected (bounding box). In this paper, we revisit perturbation-based saliency methods for object detection, with a particular focus on D-RISE, a popular model-agnostic technique. We highlight practical limitations of D-RISE, particularly the absence of a detector-specific importance score aligned with detection performance. We then propose a novel detection-loss based explainability score that quantifies the importance of each image region through the deterioration of the detector’s loss under random masking. The proposed score jointly accounts for classification confidence and localisation quality, and it is normalised to be in [0, 1], providing an interpretable per-pixel importance measure. The proposed score is evaluated on three datasets covering industrial and general-object detection scenarios. In addition to qualitative visualization, we report object-level explainability statistics and deletion-based fidelity analysis to assess the alignment between highlighted regions and detection confidence. The results indicate that the proposed $$\varDelta $$ -based scoring method produces consistent and interpretable saliency maps that are directly linked to changes in detection loss. Overall, the proposed approach establishes a principled link between visual explanations and detection performance, and paves the way for robust, quantitative comparison of XAI methods for object detection.

items.title: Exploring AI-mediated justice and fairness in collaborative learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering educational practice, yet its implications for justice and fairness in group work remain underexplored. This exploratory qualitative study examines 28 anonymous written responses collected from a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) on AI pedagogy and well-being involving higher-education students from five European universities. Participants responded to an open-ended question about how AI affects justice or fairness in education and group work. Using inductive thematic analysis and multi-label coding, the study identified recurring concerns around access, learning support, group-work support, contribution visibility, bias, agency, transparency and assessment. The findings should be read as a pilot mapping of fairness-related perceptions within this specific educational context rather than as representative evidence. We synthesise these perceptions into six preliminary dimensions of AI-mediated collaborative justice: access, contribution, assessment, epistemic and linguistic, agency, and transparency justice. The framework provides a starting point for future research and for the design of fairer AI-supported collaborative learning.

items.title: Exploring Trust Calibration in XAI - The Impact of Exposing Model Limitations to Lay Users
items.abstract: Trust calibration—aligning user trust judgment with model capability—is crucial for safe deployment of explainable AI (XAI), yet is often evaluated via global trust ratings detached from objective performance evidence. We present a preregistered, incentivized between-subject online study (N = 418 representative UK sample) on explainable skin-lesion classification that disentangles expectation-setting from experienced performance. Participants completed 15 case evaluations using a fixed XAI panel (malignancy score, reliability score, and saliency map). We systematically manipulated five experimental onboarding conditions varying example-based information and limitation disclosures with five stimulus packages naturally varying observed prediction quality. Calibration was operationalized as the deviation between trust-related judgments (TAIS and case-wise ratings) and objective performance benchmarks for the encountered cases, analysed with hierarchical mixed-effects models. Only limitation disclosure for case-wise measures reliably impacts trust calibration, and short-term experience did not yield progressive calibration. Further, the experienced package of stimuli explained substantially more variance than the experimental manipulation. However, participants were hard-pressed to differentiate between case-wise perceived trust, trustworthiness, and accuracy estimation. We discuss implications for designing limitation communication and for measuring and analysing calibration metrics in XAI evaluations. All study materials and data of this study are publicly available for replication and further academic use.

items.title: Extended Reality-Assisted Exoscopic Cervical Laminoplasty Integrating Intraoperative CT Navigation: A Technical Note on a Surgeon-Centered Virtual Workspace
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: In exoscopic spine surgery, the exoscopic image, navigation, and reference imaging occupy separate monitors. We describe a surgeon-centered extended reality (XR) workspace that places these sources in a single consumer head-mounted display, and report its measured video delay and its use in one clinical case. Methods: The stereoscopic output of a 4K three-dimensional (3D) exoscope and the intraoperative computed tomography (CT) navigation display were streamed over a dedicated local network to an Apple Vision Pro, together with four locally rendered reference layers; the exoscopic image was delivered at 1920 × 1080 in side-by-side stereoscopic format, that is, 960 × 1080 per eye. The delay of each streamed image relative to its native display was measured at the mirrored output with a 240-frames/s high-speed camera. The system was used during exoscopic minimally invasive open-door laminoplasty through a 3-cm incision for multilevel cervical ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. Results: The head-mounted exoscopic image lagged the native monitor by 30.8 ± 2.3 ms (range, 29.2–33.3 ms; n = 5), and the navigation image by 49.2 ± 1.9 ms (range, 45.8–50.0 ms; n = 5). The headset was worn for approximately 100 min without adjustment, malfunction, or reversion to the fallback monitor, and the procedure was completed without complication. Conclusions: The configuration was technically feasible with a small, measured delay. No ergonomic, workload, or clinical benefit is claimed.

items.abstract: BackgroundDriving rehabilitation increasingly incorporates eye tracking to quantify visual-cognitive performance; however, its clinical relevance and patterns of use remain unclear.PurposeThis scoping review maps how eye-tracking technologies, metrics, and applications are used in driving assessment and rehabilitation, and characterizes the populations studied.MethodFollowing Arksey and O'Malley's framework and PRISMA-ScR, five databases were searched (January 2001-July 2026). Thirty-nine eligible studies were charted for population, driving task, eye-tracking metrics, and device type.FindingsStudy populations included older adults (24 studies), autism spectrum disorder (5), traumatic brain injury (3), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (3), visual field impairment (3), and stroke (1). Eye tracking was applied to hazard perception, visual exploration and scanning, visual-motor coordination, and cognitive workload. Simulator studies mostly used remote screen- or dashboard-mounted systems, whereas on-road studies mostly used head-mounted systems. Drivers in several populations showed delayed first fixation on hazards, fewer fixations on relevant targets, and narrower or spatially biased visual search than comparison drivers.ConclusionThese population-specific gaze signatures indicate that eye tracking offers an ecologically relevant complement to occupational therapy driving assessment. Normative gaze datasets, standardized reporting, and validated clinical thresholds are needed before eye-movement metrics can guide routine return-to-drive decisions.

items.title: Faculty Adoption and Implementation Experiences During an AI Instructional Tool Pilot Test
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities and challenges for instructional practice, prompting universities to explore AI-enabled tools through structured pilot initiatives. This case study examined why faculty in the College of Agricultural and Life Science at the University of Florida chose to participate in a pilot of an AI-supported writing feedback tool and how they experienced its implementation over the course of a semester. A faculty focus group captured their motivations, perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations for future pilots. The Theory of Planned Behavior and Diffusion of Innovations theory provided a guiding framework for interpreting faculty beliefs, social influences, and perceptions of the tool’s attributes. Findings indicated that faculty were motivated by curiosity, perceived instructional value, and alignment with institutional priorities. Implementation experiences were shaped by tool usability, course fit considerations, student response, and the availability of timely support. Participants emphasized the importance of clear onboarding, transparent communication with students, and opportunities for low‑stakes experimentation. Recommendations included strengthening training, improving integration with existing systems, and establishing ongoing feedback loops between faculty and instructional support units. items.title: Faithful but Wrong: Validating LLM Faithfulness Judges for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Under Corrupted Context
items.abstract: LLM-judged faithfulness is widely used to certify RAG answers, yet it is rarely checked against human labels, and it is unclear what it rewards when the retrieved context is wrong. We measure faithfulness, correctness, refusal, and adoption of injected falsehoods on the same answers under controlled context perturbations, and audit the faithfulness judge against two human annotators. From SQuAD v2.0 we build 75 answerable and 20 unanswerable questions, with six context conditions for answerable questions (clean, random distractors, related distractors, heavy noise, contradictory evidence, answer-absent) and three prompt mitigations. Three open-weight generators (Qwen3-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Llama-3.1-8B) produce 4,230 context-conditioned answers, scored with Ragas by a local 27B judge and rule-based checks, plus two cross-family API judges (Gemini, Claude). For Qwen3-8B, distractors had no large effect (equivalent to zero within +/-10 points under lenient matching). In all three models, a contradictory passage was the damaging perturbation: under baseline and refusal prompts, correctness fell by 20-35 points and models repeated the injected falsehood in 23-48% of answers, almost never flagging the conflict. The local judge rated 86-94% of these answers faithful. Human annotators agreed closely with each other (kappa = 0.96 on supported versus not supported). Re-weighted within each condition, the local judge agreed with humans on 91-92% of Qwen3-8B answers (kappa = 0.62-0.69), but its errors concentrated in its unfaithful verdicts. Gemini and Haiku had numerically higher agreement on the same answers, though not significantly so. A judge that mostly agrees with humans about grounding can still certify a wrong answer, so faithfulness judgments cannot stand in for correctness. The effect of prompt mitigations depends on the model.

items.title: Feasibility of Augmented Reality-Guided Robotic Ultrasound with Cone-Beam CT Integration for Spine Procedures
items.abstract: Needle placement in spine interventions is critical for effective pain management, yet it depends on reliable identification of anatomical landmarks and careful trajectory planning. Conventional imaging guidance often relies on both computed tomography (CT) and X-ray fluoroscopy, exposing patients and staff to high doses of radiation while providing limited real-time 3D feedback. The choice of visualization may also affect operator performance and cognitive workload. We present an optical see-through augmented reality (OST-AR)–guided robotic system for spine procedures that provides in situ visualization of spinal structures to support needle trajectory planning. We integrate a cone-beam CT (CBCT)-derived 3D spine model, which is co-registered with live ultrasound, enabling users to combine global anatomical context with local, real-time imaging. We evaluated the system in a phantom user study involving two representative spine procedures: facet joint injection and lumbar puncture. Sixteen participants performed insertions under two visualization conditions: conventional screen vs. AR. Results show that AR significantly reduces execution time and across-task placement error, while also improving usability, trust, and spatial understanding, and lowering cognitive workload. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of AR-guided robotic ultrasound for spine interventions, highlighting its potential to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and user experience in image-guided procedures.

items.title: Feedback on feedback: Student use of AI to interpret educator feedback
items.abstract: The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students engage with learning and feedback in higher education. While existing research has largely focused on AI-generated feedback and hybrid human–AI feedback approaches, less is known about how students independently use AI to interpret educator feedback. This study investigated how Computer Science students use GenAI tools to understand and act upon educator feedback. Drawing on feedback literacy theory, an exploratory mixed-methods survey was conducted with 140 undergraduate and postgraduate Computer Science students at an Australian university. Overall, 89.0% of respondents reported using AI at least occasionally to interpret educator feedback, primarily to explain unclear comments and suggest improvements. Although students generally perceived AI explanations positively, many also recognised that AI could occasionally misunderstand educator intentions. The study contributes to emerging discussions on AI-mediated feedback literacy by conceptualising generative AI as an intermediary interpretive layer between educator feedback and student action, with implications for feedback design and the development of critical AI literacy in higher education.

items.title: Ferdinand Tönnies and the Sociological Roots of Dual-Process Theories of Thinking: Cognition, Social Relations, and Modernity
items.abstract: Dual-process theories of thinking occupy an important place in contemporary psychology, economics, and cognitive sociology. They distinguish intuitive activities, often rapid and involving little deliberation, from more controlled and reflective activities. Similar distinctions were already present in classical psychology and sociology. This article revisits that intellectual history through Ferdinand Tönnies, who distinguishes organic will (Wesenwille) from rational will (Kürwille) and relates them to communal and societal relations. We show how this theory corresponds to contemporary research and how its ambition to explain psychological activities and social forms together can enrich that research. We then discuss three limitations of certain historical interpretations offered by Tönnies: the naturalisation of differences between the sexes, the association of reflection with modernity, and the association of calculation with market relations. This discussion leads us to examine modernity as a transformation of the social conditions under which intuitive and reflective activities develop and are exercised. To this end, we propose four complementary dimensions: the cultivation, mobilisation, social distribution, and sociotechnical delegation of cognitive activities. The framework examines how institutions shape cognitive learning, judgement, and recognition, while the activities thereby organised contribute in turn to the reproduction and transformation of the social relations within which they occur.
